article.title: Modular Ships Mojo 1.0, Locking In API Stability for the AI Systems Language
article.summary: Modular released Mojo 1.0 on August 11, 2026, committing to backward-compatible, mostly-additive changes three years after the language's 2023 debut.
article.body_markdown:
## Overview

Modular released version 1.0 of Mojo on August 11, 2026, according to [Modular's official blog](https://www.modular.com/blog/modular-26-5-mojo-1-0-is-here) and the project's own [release notes](https://mojolang.org/releases/v1.0.0/). The release marks Mojo's transition from an evolving beta into what [The Register](https://www.theregister.com/ai-and-ml/2026/08/12/modulars-mojo-programming-language-hits-10-milestone/5286545) described as "a stable, production-ready, general-purpose programming language," three years after Mojo's public debut, which [The Register](https://www.theregister.com/ai-and-ml/2026/08/12/modulars-mojo-programming-language-hits-10-milestone/5286545) and [Linuxiac](https://linuxiac.com/mojo-1-0-programming-language-officially-released/) both date to 2023.

As [previously reported](/article/2026-05/25-mojo-10-beta-arrives-as-modular-declares-the-ai-native-systems-language-feature-complete), Modular shipped Mojo's first beta, v1.0.0b1, in May, explicitly breaking compatibility with earlier code to clean up the language ahead of a stable release. The 1.0 release now formalizes the stability promise that beta was building toward.

## What We Know

### A Formal Stability Commitment

Mojo's release notes state that "during the 1.x timeframe, changes should mostly be additive," adding that "we may still make breaking changes, but they'll be managed with care," according to [Mojo's official release notes](https://mojolang.org/releases/v1.0.0/). Modular's blog post frames the same commitment slightly differently, stating that changes "should primarily be additive, giving developers confidence that the language will not continually shift beneath them," per [Modular's blog](https://www.modular.com/blog/modular-26-5-mojo-1-0-is-here).

### What Changed From the Beta

The 1.0 release carries a further round of breaking changes on top of the May beta. Destructors were renamed from `__del__()` to `__deinit__()` for consistency with `__init__()`, according to [Mojo's release notes](https://mojolang.org/releases/v1.0.0/). The `InlineArray` type was renamed to `Array`, with its `ElementType` parameter renamed to `T` and `size` renamed to `length`, and `StringSlice` was renamed to `StringSpan`, the release notes state. `Pointer` and `UnsafePointer` were unified into a single `Pointer` type, with unsafe operations now prefixed `unsafe_`, per the [release notes](https://mojolang.org/releases/v1.0.0/) — a change Modular's blog describes more broadly as making Mojo's pointer handling consist of "a single Pointer type," according to [Modular's blog](https://www.modular.com/blog/modular-26-5-mojo-1-0-is-here).

Variables "are now consistently declared with var," [Modular's blog](https://www.modular.com/blog/modular-26-5-mojo-1-0-is-here) states, a change [Linuxiac](https://linuxiac.com/mojo-1-0-programming-language-officially-released/) corroborates, reporting that "variables are now consistently declared using `var`." Mojo also gained Python-style lambda syntax for inline closures, according to both [Modular](https://www.modular.com/blog/modular-26-5-mojo-1-0-is-here) and [Linuxiac](https://linuxiac.com/mojo-1-0-programming-language-officially-released/), and the compiler "now diagnoses memory safety problems involving reference invalidation," per [Modular's blog](https://www.modular.com/blog/modular-26-5-mojo-1-0-is-here) — described by Linuxiac as improved "memory-safety diagnostics" that can "detect problems involving invalidated references," according to [Linuxiac](https://linuxiac.com/mojo-1-0-programming-language-officially-released/).

Other behavioral changes in the release notes include list expressions now constructing `Array` instead of `List` by default, string iteration yielding grapheme clusters by default, and invalid slice indexing now aborting instead of silently clamping, according to [Mojo's release notes](https://mojolang.org/releases/v1.0.0/).

### Standard Library Licensing and the Compiler Roadmap

The Mojo standard library is available under the Apache License v2.0 with LLVM Exceptions, according to [The Register](https://www.theregister.com/ai-and-ml/2026/08/12/modulars-mojo-programming-language-hits-10-milestone/5286545). The compiler itself remains closed; Modular says "our commitment remains unchanged – we will open source the Mojo compiler and toolchain in 2026," according to [Modular's blog](https://www.modular.com/blog/modular-26-5-mojo-1-0-is-here), a plan [The Register](https://www.theregister.com/ai-and-ml/2026/08/12/modulars-mojo-programming-language-hits-10-milestone/5286545) also reported, noting the company "intends to release the Mojo compiler as open source this year."

### Mojo's Creator and Qualcomm's Ownership

Mojo's public development has been led by Chris Lattner, described by [The Register](https://www.theregister.com/ai-and-ml/2026/08/12/modulars-mojo-programming-language-hits-10-milestone/5286545) as the "creator of LLVM, the Clang compiler, Swift programming language, and MLIR compiler infrastructure," who co-founded Modular and "has led Mojo's public development since 2023." The 1.0 release arrives with Modular now under Qualcomm's ownership: [The Register](https://www.theregister.com/ai-and-ml/2026/08/12/modulars-mojo-programming-language-hits-10-milestone/5286545) reported that "Modular was acquired by Qualcomm in June 2026," and Modular's own blog post is copyrighted to "Modular Inc, A Qualcomm Company," according to [Modular's blog](https://www.modular.com/blog/modular-26-5-mojo-1-0-is-here). As [previously reported](/article/2026-06/25-qualcomm-to-buy-ai-software-startup-modular-for-about-39-billion-taking-aim-at-nvidias-cuda-moat), Qualcomm agreed in June to acquire Modular in an all-stock deal.

Asked about the risk of competitors interfering with Mojo and Modular's MAX platform now that Modular sits inside a chipmaker, Lattner said: "They both contribute an incredible amount to open source code. So I don't expect there to be any problem here," according to [The Register](https://www.theregister.com/ai-and-ml/2026/08/12/modulars-mojo-programming-language-hits-10-milestone/5286545).

## What We Don't Know

Modular has not given an exact date for open-sourcing the Mojo compiler and toolchain beyond "this year," per [Modular's blog](https://www.modular.com/blog/modular-26-5-mojo-1-0-is-here). Neither Modular nor The Register specified a precise closing date for the Qualcomm acquisition; Modular's June announcement had projected a close in the second half of 2026.

## Analysis

The 1.0 release closes a stability gap that has followed Mojo since its 2023 debut: a language pitched as combining Python's usability with systems-level performance, but one that developers could not build long-term production code on top of without expecting breaking changes at every release. By formalizing a mostly-additive change policy for the 1.x line, Modular is betting that API stability — not new features — is what unlocks broader enterprise adoption of a language still overwhelmingly used within its own AI inference stack. That bet now plays out with Modular operating as a Qualcomm subsidiary, adding a new set of questions about how a chipmaker's ownership of a hardware-neutral programming language and inference platform will be perceived by the same multi-vendor developer base Modular has spent years courting.
